utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in the courtroom and also those just outside assisting us. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-00-39-T, the Prosecutor versus Momcilo Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say Mr. Jonovic, Andrej Jonovic, has returned to the case. He has been away learning some law in London, which is never a bad thing, but he's back here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber does not express itself whether London is a better place to learn the law than any other place in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Nor will we, Your Honour, for this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But nevertheless, welcome back, Mr. Jonovic. Mr. Harmon, are you ready to proceed?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I would even have almost already expected you to remind me that I should remind you that you're still bound by the solemn declaration you gave at the beginning of your testimony, but that even goes without saying; nevertheless I say it. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we are still on the topic of the arming of the Bosnian Serbs prior to the 12th of May and your knowledge about that. Yesterday, you testified in the third session of the hearing that you were aware of two affairs in which Serbs had been blamed where it had do with trucks full of weapons that were captured. There was a debate in the Assembly about this problem. "So it was not totally unknown that there was some kind of arming, but I didn't want to get involved in that kind of thing." That, I believe, is found, Your Honours, at page 47 of the transcript yesterday. I have a time cite of 18:28:53. Mr. Krajisnik, did one of those incidents in which Serbs were involved in arming involve an SDS member of the BH parliament by the name of Dusan Kozic?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said there was a debate in the Assembly. Not an official one, though, regarding a truck that came precisely from Herzegovina and ultimately ended up, allegedly, in the Bileca barracks, but it was not an official debate. Now, was it Kozic or somebody else, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I know that it was discussed at the Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me pass out two exhibits. These are -- Your Honours don't have. These -- once they're distributed, I will need a number on each.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While these documents are distributed, Mr. Harmon, the passage you just referred to appears in my transcript at page 25275, last few lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the first document, which seems to be press clipping with the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I have the other -- the other document numbered first? I'll be using that one first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Then the report on the uncovering of the smuggling of weapons into Bosnia-Herzegovina will have number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1213, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the other document, which seems to be a press clipping, the title in bold being "Karadzic Against America Too" would be number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1214, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'm going to be referring first to the report on the uncovering of the smuggling of weapons into Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is Exhibit P1213, and I would like to direct your attention and the Court's attention -- first of all the Court's attention to page 2 of the document, the second and --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I've never seen any one of these documents before, and I was not kept abreast of these writings.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that there was an extra-parliamentary debate. I'm just saying that I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me -- let me, first of all, identify these documents and direct your attention and the Court's attention to the appropriate passages. Take your time and examine the P1213.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm going to be referring principally to the passages that are found starting at the second paragraph, page 2 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, for your information, in the B/C/S version I'm principally going to be focusing your attention on the first page, the last paragraph, going over to the second paragraph -- second page through the first full paragraph on the second page. But after you have a chance to review those documents, please let me know, and I will proceed in asking you some questions about them.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just these two paragraphs, is that what you're saying? I really should have had a look at this information. I haven't seen it before. As for this particular case, yes, we discussed it in the Assembly. I mean, yes. Extra-parliamentary debate. That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, familiarise yourself with that document, principally the passages starting from the beginning and through the passages I've mentioned to you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is a report from the Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo relating to an event that occurred on the 24th of May, 1991, and if we turn to the actual incident itself you can see that a vehicle that was driven by a Milutin Popovic was stopped, and present in that car was Dusan Kozic. Now, first of all, Dusan Kozic was an SDS member of the Bosnian parliament, wasn't he?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Shortly after this incident in July, Dusan Kozic was elected to the SDS Main Board along with you; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he was still a Member of Parliament. I mean, I don't know whether he was elected. Probably so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'll show you a document and you can confirm whether he was elected or not.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I mean I believe you, but he was an MP throughout.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes. He's also a member -- thereafter he was also a member of the SDS Main Board, with you.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But he was in the SDS before that as well, before July, 1991. It wasn't that he became that only then. As far as I know, he was a member of the Main Board.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: And before --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You've answered my question then. In this incident, Mr. Krajisnik, you can see that the vehicle in which Mr. Kozic was a passenger contained eight crates of rifles, each containing 10 Russian-made automatic rifles, containing 16.800 bullets, it contained a pistol, it contained 78 pistol cartridges. And at the scene of the detention and stop, Mr. Kozic requested immunity, parliamentary immunity in this incident. Now, you, Mr. Krajisnik, were the president of the Assembly. A member of your party was arrested on serious charges, or at least detained on serious charges, the smuggling of eight crates of automatic weapons. Did that matter concern you as the president of the Assembly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything about this. I didn't know that he had been stopped or that he was seeking immunity, nothing. I'll tell you what people were saying at the Assembly, but this I hadn't had the opportunity of -- well, it has nothing to do with me. He's an MP in the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So how did you become aware of this incident, then, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm telling you. We had a session of the Assembly, and then deputies in the corridors started discussing this. "You Serbs are arming yourselves," and I didn't hear of any investigation or criminal charges or arrest or anything. I heard of nothing, and I didn't even know it was Kozic. I just knew that there was some case in Bileca that allegedly some army weapons were there. Perhaps it was this way, but I don't know. I heard of a similar case, though, similar to what you've been telling me, that this truck was stopped, the one coming from Montenegro. Actually, I heard this from the Muslims. From Muslim deputies, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, I want to focus on Mr. Kozic because he was a member of your party. Did the event give rise to any discussions in the SDS Deputies' Club?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no discussion about this, and this person was not identified as Kozic. Now I see it's Kozic. Well, probably it was. I don't know about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, in May of 1991, would it have been -- and given the political situation both in Croatia and eminent difficult situation in Bosnia, would the fact that eight cartons -- eight crates of weapons were being smuggled by an SDS Member of Parliament would have been something that would have been noteworthy? Would it have been something that would have been serious?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, if it is serious -- well, of course it's serious, but if that was true, then there was a procedure that should have been initiated. That is to say for having this MP's immunity removed, to have this discussed before parliament, et cetera. That's the procedure. What I am supposed to do with an MP who is a suspect? If something like this was actually done, then immunity should have been removed, but nobody did that. Or, rather, those who knew about it didn't do anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I'd like to turn your attention to P1214, the next exhibit that's in front of you, and I want to direct your attention to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we do so, Mr. Harmon. Mr. Krajisnik, you earlier said, "... we discussed it in the Assembly. I mean ... extra-parliamentary debate." What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when the Prosecutor asked me about whether I had ever been informed about the Serbs arming themselves, I said that I had heard an unofficial discussion. You know, before the debate, before the session. I heard that there was such a case in Herzegovina. And deputies talk the way they talk. Everybody talks in his own way. So this was not before the Assembly and no measures were taken. And then I said there were these two cases. That's what I meant. We kept blaming them and they kept blaming us. I know MPs did that. I know of two cases where Serbs were being blamed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you didn't say, "We discussed it in the Assembly extra-parliamentary debate." Did you say "we" or did you say others or -- I mean, I'm just trying to find out how to understand your testimony, and also perhaps I'd like to verify what you exactly said in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that that is when I learned about this, that the MPs were discussing this amongst --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I was asking you what you said in this court. I mean, that's what you explained, but I'd like to know from you whether you said we discussed it whether this is an error in translation and that you did say something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I always use this term "we." I meant our side, you see. Well, I probably said "we," yes. But I use "we" in the sense of our side. I meant our MPs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you called that an extra-parliamentary debate, and you now explain that this was an informal discussion you heard about of MPs discussing matters, well, let's say in the corridors. Is that a correct understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. At that Assembly, that is to say in this environment, I heard about this, that the MPs amongst themselves were mentioning this case, and that is when I learned of it. However, this was a daily occurrence, these mutual accusations, and I didn't pay any attention to it because other side was accusing the other side the previous day, for instance. But I said that I heard of these two cases.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Did you use the words -- I mean, "extra-parliamentary debate," is that correctly translated or ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did say "extra-parliamentary debate." It is not a debate, though. It is as you enter the hall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You explained that already. I just wanted to know what words you used.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Judge Hanoteau has a question for you as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Krajisnik, you said yesterday, "[In English] There was a debate in the Assembly about this problem." [Interpretation] And you've added, "[In English] So it is not that it was totally unknown that there was some kind of arming but I didn't want to get involved in that kind of thing." [Interpretation] This is what you said yesterday. First of all, if I understood you correctly, today you're telling us that there was no debate at the Assembly; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was not at the session, Your Honour. But you know what it's like; two hours before the session the MPs meet up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... I'm just asking you to tell me the following: Within the walls of that room, did you discuss this topic? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean at the session. Let me just check that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm talking about that place where all the deputies meet.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Well, it was among the deputies that this was being discussed, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it was not in a hallway. It was not a conversation that took place in the corridor, in a hallway.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the corridors, yes, in the "couloirs," yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Second question, Mr. Krajisnik: "[In English] I didn't want to get involved in that kind of thing." [Interpretation] What does this mean, "I did not want to get involved in that kind of thing"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's quite simple, Your Honour. Every day there were accusations levelled at different sides, and I wanted the institutions to deal with that. Why am I supposed to infer something, and why am I supposed to ask whether the rumours are correct? There's the MUP, there's the government; let them resolve it. That's what I did both in the case of Muslims and in the case of Serbs. I just learned about it, heard about it, sort of like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So it does not mean that you were not particularly interested in the topic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Well, how should I put it? It wasn't that I wasn't particularly interested, but I just didn't pay much attention because this was a daily topic. Well, not a daily topic, but sort of. There were these accusations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HANOTEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, if you could turn your attention to P1214.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honours, I direct your attention to the middle paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And, Mr. Krajisnik, this is a very short article. I'm principally concerned in the text that starts at the top of the second column, the column to the right, and goes down approximately nine lines, eight lines. The text which I will read into the record, this is attributed to Dr. Karadzic at a press conference. The text reads: "SDS claims that the weapons that were transported through Bileca were trophy weapons and that it was only coincidence that the SDS deputy in the BH Assembly, Dusan Kozic, found himself there. Karadzic thinks it is also a conspiracy of anti-Serbian media." First question, Mr. Krajisnik: Is the term "trophy weapons," are you familiar with that term, and can you explain to the Court what that term means in your language?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Trophy weapons is if you have weapons -- well, if you have, say, a trophy from the Second World War, and then you keep it at home as a memento. It can be used but it's not some kind of modern weapon. I mean, that is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So Dr. Karadzic is explaining to the public through this press conference that these eight crates of 10 Russian-made automatic weapons are trophy weapons. Is that how you interpret this text?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot interpret this. I don't know anything about it. I don't know why he said this. And I don't know whether there were eight crates and whether these were trophy weapons. I cannot interpret that. I don't even know what kind of weapons. Some kind of Russian-made weapons, if that's what this report says. Russian-made -- I mean, Russian automatic rifles were not modern weapons. I know. Those are the ones that have drums. But that is really old fashioned, like from the Second World War, if what the report says is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You mean if what Dr. Karadzic says is correct.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That information where it says Russian automatic weapons, those are the ones with drums, an old-fashioned weapon. As far as I managed to read this, I think that is what it says here. I can have a look.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: May I then ask you one additional question,

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Is it your testimony that Russian automatic weapons were not produced after the Second World War?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. The Russian automatic weapons that I saw were the ones with drums at our theatres of war. I don't know when they were manufactured, but that's what the soldiers told me. That was their explanation given to me. These automatic weapons with drums, if I read that here, if I read that they were Russian automatic weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So now I have to understand your testimony to be that where the article says that it was Russian automatic weapons --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Russian made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That you are acquainted only with Russian automatic weapons that originate from the Second World War, without having any knowledge on whether, later on, automatic weapons were produced.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no. No. No. Mr. President, on the second page of this information, I read this, there were 10 automatic rifles, Russian made. In eight crates with 10 rifles respectively. That's what I read in the information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, "The information where it says Russian automatic weapons, those are the ones with drums, drums, an old-fashioned weapon. As far as I manage to read this, this is what it says here." From what I understand, the article only says "Russian automatic weapons." You interpret that as being the Russian automatic weapons as you told us you are familiar with that are the ones with drums originating from the Second World War. Therefore, my question was whether you are aware of any later produced Russian automatic weapons in order to see what makes you interpret this information as relating to very old-fashioned weapons rather than any other weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the first information says in 10 crates there were Russian automatic weapons. That's what it says in the first information. Russian made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It even says automatic rifles, but apart from that detail, yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't know --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. No. No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Have I got this wrong? There is no reference to Russian in the newspaper article.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I'm talking about the report. Perhaps that's the confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Because the cross-examination was about the newspaper article at this particular juncture.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Then I have to -- let me then focus on that. That's good that you draw my attention to it. Let me just see. Yes. Nevertheless, Mr. Krajisnik referred to Russian rifles, apparently referring to the other document. I mean, I did not invent your answer, Mr. Krajisnik, that you were talking about Russian weapons and that you explained that the Russian weapons were the old-fashioned ones with drums. It's totally unclear to me on what basis you conclude, when talking about Russian automatic weapons, why you conclude that these were the old-fashioned ones rather than anything produced since 1945.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Your Honour. In the first brief it's clearly written, "Eight crates containing 10 automatic weapons of Russian make each." Not automatic rifles. I know that what we used in the last -- in the World War II, that there were those rifles with drums. Automatic rifles are a modern thing, and automatic weapons that I knew were those ones with drums from World War II. I mean, I don't actually know, I'm just interpreting it to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, first of all, I'd like to have this checked on whether it says rifles or -- perhaps we could have the original --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could I make one other observation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Part of the problem may be that in his question my learned friend Mr. Harmon, referring clearly to the newspaper article, said so Dr. Karadzic is explaining to the public through this press conference that these eight crates of 10 Russian-made automatic weapons are trophy weapons," and of course, as I've observed, the newspaper article doesn't say that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I do understand that, but since the answer referred also to automatic weapons and gave an interpretation of what those weapons would have been, I put my question in relation to that answer. But let's first check whether it says -- could we have the original, second page, where it reads -- Madam Usher, could you -- that's the second page. Could I draw the attention approximately the middle of the page. For the interpreters, it reads "sa po 10 automata ruske" and then a word which I can't pronounce. Does that say rifles or weapons, or perhaps neither of them?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: It says "automata" which means "automatic." It doesn't mean anything specific. "Automatic" can mean submachine-gun, it can mean automatic rifle. It is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it's not specified as far as the type of automatic weapon is concerned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second. Could you please then translate just the relevant line. Could I invite you then to -- perhaps someone slowly reads -- Mr. Sladojevic, could you please read the line in which both the 10, the eight, and the 16.800 appear, slowly read it, and may I invite the interpreters then to translate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLADOJEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Established that in the freight area there are eight crates containing 10 automatic weapons of Russian make each, and 16.800 rounds for those weapons."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So therefore the translation in English, where it says "rifles" gives a specification which does not appear in the original text. Nevertheless, Mr. Krajisnik, still -- because I'm coming back to my point. You interpreted this information. You went, without any further explanation, as to more or less old-fashioned weapons, and I still do not understand why you interpreted this as being weapons with drums known to you from the Second World War rather than any other automatic weapon produced in Russia since the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, during the war, Kalashnikovs were in use. Kalashnikovs are Russian-made automatic rifles. But also in use were old automatic weapons from World War II, with drums, drum barrels. And when it says "automatic weapons" in this text, it cannot mean automatic rifles. No way. In the Serbian language, when you read it, it's clear. The Russian-made automatic weapons were the ones with drum barrels. I don't know what automatic weapons are, but I'm telling you what I saw as a layman during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you then please also explain why you say it's -- you say, "From a language point of view this could not be understood as automatic rifles."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me tell you, Your Honour. I have rather little English, and when I try to find a proper translation for the word "automat," I found both "automatic rifle" and "automatic weapon." But in our language it's different, and I know how it worked in practice. "Automat" was the word used to describe this drum barrel weapon, whereas automatic rifles are something different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Should I then understand that apart from the Kalashnikov automatic rifles you referred to, that no other automatic weapons were produced in Russia since 1945?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no clue. I just know what there was in circulation in our parts. I don't know anything else. I'm just saying that those automatic weapons that were in circulation at the beginning of the war originated from World War II. Whether it's the same thing, I don't know. And I don't even know where they brought them from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I now understand why you drew that conclusion. Whether that is a conclusion which is justified by the reasons you gave is another question which we don't have to answer now. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. Why wouldn't it be justified, Your Honour? I would like to get things clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just tell me what remains unclear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Krajisnik. Well, to be quite honest, you say, "I don't have the knowledge. I don't have the knowledge." Nevertheless, you drew conclusions. That's the reason why I said this. But I left that question open, but that could be the reason for posing such question. And I'm not debating with you, Mr. Krajisnik. No, no. I gave Mr. Harmon an opportunity now to proceed. No, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon now gets -- you can do that at the end of your testimony. Mr. Harmon can put his next question. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know why there is such a problem about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the affair of Mr. Kozic and the smuggling of weapons was on the front page of Oslobodjenje on the 27th of May, 1991, as well as a reference to his invoking immunity. Were you aware that this particular incident received that sort of public notoriety?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to tell you that I'm pretty thrown at this moment, and I cannot properly answer questions because I am experiencing this as an injustice to me, that a conclusion should have been made that does not appreciate my -- my explanations. I have no idea about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. So you are unaware that this Kozic affair was on the front page of Oslobodjenje on the 27th of May. I take it that is your answer. Do I understand your answer correctly?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. Possibly. Maybe I've read -- maybe I read it before. I don't know any more. I don't know whether it was accurate or not, because I had read hundreds of articles in Oslobodjenje telling stories that were untrue. Maybe I read it and thought it was inaccurate. There was very ugly propaganda coming from all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, referring to Prosecution Exhibit 1214, Mr. Karadzic clearly was apprised of the -- what I will call the Kozic affair because he commented on this publicly. He commented directly on the event, the weapons being transported through Bileca, and that it was only a coincidence that the SDS deputy in the BH Assembly, Dusan Kozic, found himself there. Now, how is it, Mr. Krajisnik, that Mr. Karadzic knew about this affair and you did not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karadzic is not my twin brother. I didn't know, and I'm really indignant now. I cannot answer these questions any more this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. Might I endorse what Mr. Krajisnik has just said. That was a question he simply could not answer. The only result was utter speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me re-read the question. Mr. Harmon, the first question should have been, "Do you know how Mr. Karadzic knew about this?" And it appears from the answer that Mr. -- that he doesn't know, so therefore the question has been answered. Apart from -- I'm just interpreting the newspaper article. The coincidence which is mentioned -- okay, let's not further comment on that. Mr. Krajisnik has answered your question. Please proceed, Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, finally, Mr. Krajisnik, the excuse or the defence to this affair that is given by Mr. Karadzic is that he thinks it was also a conspiracy of the anti-Serbian media. I have two questions for you,

utterances.speaker: MR. KRAJISNIK
utterances.text: Was there an investigation by members of the SDS either at a party level or at any other level in parliament into this affair; and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether they conducted an investigation, and if they didn't, I don't know why they didn't. I don't know why it would have been up to them to conduct an investigation when they had official state authorities for that. This is the year 1991. For six months of that year the MUP functioned. They could have carried out an investigation. There was the public prosecutor's office. Why would it be them? I mean, I don't know. I don't understand the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think we've explored this topic enough, Mr. Krajisnik. I want to turn next to an exhibit that has been previously exhibited, and I have -- it's P37. It is a transcript, a portion of the transcript of P37. This, Mr. Krajisnik, is a transcript of the SDS Assembly session that took place on the 12th of July, 1991. I would like to direct --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Does it need a number?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, it has a number, Your Honour. I mentioned P37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: An extract from P37. Your Honours, I'm going to directs Your Honours' attention to the comments of Miro Delic, who was the president of the Bileca SDS, found at page 100, and particularly I direct Your Honours' attention from the beginning of his remarks through to the conclusion of the first paragraph on page 101.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, for your reference, I'm referring to page 89. You'll see 89 in the upper right-hand corner and you'll see, seven lines from the bottom, the comments of Miro Delic, and I want you to read, if you would, through to the end of page 90.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this speech from Mr. Delic deals with essentially a new party that has been established in his municipality, the League of Communists Movement for Yugoslavia, and he goes on to say, starting at the bottom of page 100 in the English, he said, "But that is the least important thing. In the meantime, in fact, just two days ago the party organised a conference of its members and sympathisers, officers and other Commies, I would call them, in Bileca municipality, although there are very few of them. The conference was held in the JNA club in Bileca. They raised the issue of involvement or, rather, distribution of weapons to this group as a response to the distribution of weapons in the SDS organisation." Mr. Krajisnik, were you present when those remarks were made?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't read that part about the SDS. I read till the end of page 90, but I didn't see that passage. Give me just a second, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you tell me where is it written "distribution of weapons to the SDS"? I read through the end of page 90.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's found on page 90, Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes, yes. Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: First question, Mr. Krajisnik: Were you present when Mr. Delic made his remarks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know the man, but I did attend this session of the Assembly. However, I don't remember what he said here. I do know about this party called Movement for Yugoslavia. I don't remember the man now. At that time maybe I had heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: But if these remarks were made in your presence, Mr. Krajisnik, where there's a clear and unequivocal reference to the distribution of weapons in the SDS organisation, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm trying to understand your evidence, did you hear those remarks? Do you recall those remarks?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall him saying this, but I'm not saying that he couldn't have. He must have said it, since it's recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: If we turn, Mr. Krajisnik, if we continue immediately after these remarks by this particular speaker, you speak - that's found at page 102, Mr. Krajisnik, and your version it's found at the bottom of page 91 - and you then called upon Dr. Karadzic to say something on the topic, although he has already presented the position on that in his report. Dr. Karadzic then addresses the assembled SDS deputies, and we can find his remarks on page 92, Mr. Krajisnik, and in particular I direct your attention to the paragraph, middle of the page, starting with "Me --" it looks like "yes, no." And, Your Honours, I direct your attention to page 102, the last paragraph. Given those remarks were significant, Mr. Krajisnik, you directed Dr. Karadzic to respond, and Dr. Karadzic in fact did respond, and he said the following: "We have said clearly that we will not be creating any party armies. We know that Serbs are arming themselves with smuggled weapons and some ancient ones. We as a party do not have the right to arm the people, but we do not have the right to discourage it either, because we could lead it into a position so difficult it could result in its suffering." Do you recall those remarks of Dr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. I'm not the chairman here. Somebody else chaired that session.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well, who was that, then? If I've made a mistake, I'll stand corrected.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somebody else chaired the session when Mr. Karadzic made his contribution. This was a party gathering.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... I'll stand corrected. My question, nevertheless, remains the same: Did you hear the remarks of Dr. Karadzic that I just read to you?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He may have said that. I'm not ruling out that possibility. Maybe I even heard it. Okay, let's say I heard it, but what then? I don't understand the question. Let's assume that I did hear him say this. I tried to explain that discussion and debate was going on in all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, saying that everybody was arming themselves, and I already explained two specific examples. His remarks here are of a general nature, nothing specific. It was common knowledge that Bosnia is full of weapons. I did see later that Serbs had weapons, but I don't know in which way they were supplied and who supplied them. Whether those were smuggling channels or private sales, and I saw later during the war that they had weapons, including those of the Yugoslav People's Army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, at this particular session of the SDS Assembly on the 12th of July, 45 members were elected to the Main Board of the SDS. You can see that at -- Your Honours, at page -- starting at 125 of the English. And, Mr. Krajisnik, in the B/C/S version, you'll see that on the last page of the document. Mr. Krajisnik, you were elected to the SDS Main Board, as it says. Mr. Jovan Tintor and Danilo Veselinovic were elected. Both of those persons elected to the SDS Main Board represented Sarajevo, did they not?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, they are from Sarajevo, but there are many others among them who are from Sarajevo: Ratko Adzic, Jovo Jovanovic, Jovan Sarac, Neskovic, Toholj; all of them are men from Sarajevo, and the two that you mentioned are.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I'm only asking you about the two. In addition, Rajko Dukic, number 35, Goran Zugic, number 36, those people from the Birac area, the area where Mr. Deronjic came from; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We know from the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are from Birac, yes, from Milici, and Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We also know from the examination of this document that Mr. Deronjic was present because he was one of the speakers. And he stood for election, but he did not gain a seat on the Main Board, at least in 1991. He subsequently did in 1993. And finally, the man we've been talking when, Dusko Kozic, is number 44 on this document, Mr. Krajisnik. Now, the Trial Chamber, Mr. Krajisnik, has heard evidence that Messrs. Tintor, Veselinovic, Dukic, Zugic, Deronjic, and now Mr. Kozic were involved in the smuggling of arms to Serbian citizens prior to the commencement of the war. Did you at any time, Mr. Krajisnik, have a conversation with any of those co-members of the SDS Main Board and discuss the topic of the arming of Bosnian Serbs prior to the 12th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I told you that I didn't know in which way Serbs were arming themselves. I told you the extent of my knowledge concerning two cases that were talked about, although they were never brought to trial, that represented an indication that Serbs were getting hold of weapons in some way. How, I don't know. And that's, in truth, all my knowledge about arms supplies. Not a single piece of weaponry reached my village, because I've told you already if I could have, if I had been involved in that, my village would have been the first on my list.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I know that your village was important to you. I know that Sarajevo, from the evidence that I've heard so far, was very, very important to you personally because your family roots were from the Novi Grad municipality, from Rajlovac, and I know also politically Sarajevo was considered important by the Bosnian Serbs. So I know you took a keen interest in the events in that municipality. That's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, you're taking the wrong path. I have nothing to do with Jovan Tintor or Veselinovic or whatever they stated here. Please, let's not waste any more time. Sarajevo is important to me. Rajlovac is important to me. Zabrdje is important to me. No problem whatsoever. I know exactly what you're getting at, but please, this has nothing to do anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's -- Mr. Krajisnik, let's turn to tab 120. If Mr. Krajisnik could be given the bundle we had yesterday. Tab 120, Your Honours, is Exhibit P825, tab 5. Mr. Krajisnik, as soon as it's given to you. In the meantime, Your Honours, I'm going to address Your Honours' attention to the bottom -- the last paragraph at the bottom of page 1 in the English. And, Mr. Krajisnik, the page -- the paragraph I want to direct your attention to is on page 2. It is the second complete paragraph on page 2. And the document, Your Honour, is a document that is dated the 20th of September, 1993, and it is a document that is --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you could just tell me where the beginning is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krajisnik. I'm referring to page 2 of the document, and it says "Pocetkom 1991."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a document, Your Honour, from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Internal Affairs, Serbian public security station in Ilidza. The author of this document is a man who is the chief of the public security station in Ilidza, Tihomir Glavas. It is dated the 20th of September, 1993, and it is in part a retrospective document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this document -- I'll read the paragraph I am interested in. "At the beginning of 1991, during illegal meetings organised by Kovac Tomislav, Commander of the Ilidza public security station at the time, policemen of Serbian nationality were informed that the war option for realisation of national interests was being increasingly promoted. Aside from the obligation that Serbs gather up and prepare for war through those meetings that took place in Dobrinja, Ilidza and Blazuj, it was also agreed that intense activity should be undertaken to arm citizens of Serbian nationality. Armament was transported from Ravna Romanija, Pale, Sokolac, Kalinovik, the village of Nedavici, Trnovo, village of Tosici, Hadzici, Jusuf Dzonlagici barracks, Lukavica, and Nedzarici." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, how far is Ilidza from your home village of Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Five or six kilometres, perhaps eight kilometres, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And how far is Hadzici from your home village in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, about 20 -- say, 15 to 20 kilometres. I can't say exactly. From Zabrdje to -- well, I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this document, Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, do you know -- did you know Tomislav Kovac prior to the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe I met him once. Maybe -- just a moment, please. Yes, yes. Yes. I did know him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I hardly saw him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, this -- this document -- this report discusses a -- essentially a -- essentially an intensive arming programme, starting in the beginning of 1991. And as we know, Mr. Krajisnik, from the concerns of the Serbian people, from the leadership, that they had paramount concerns about genocide and being victims of genocide once again. Mr. Krajisnik, we've seen another document, and I'm going to show it to you in a few minutes. It's the key that was attached to the report prepared by General Kukanjac on the 20th of March. That's P51. I'll show it to you in a few minutes. But the key to that report, the addendum to that report, indicates that in Ilidza 2.800 weapons were distributed, and in Hadzici 1.500 weapons were distributed. The distribution of those weapons was both through the JNA and through the SDS party. Now, Mr. Krajisnik, were you aware that in the municipality that was adjacent to your home there was the distribution of arms to Serb citizens beginning in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I have already answered that I did not know. I did not know about the way in which they were being armed. I told you what I knew then. I was then the president of the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let me turn to a different document, then, Mr. Krajisnik. This is found at tab 118, Mr. Krajisnik. I want to take you through -- very quickly through a series of documents. Tab 118 has an exhibit number, Mr. Krajisnik. It's P529, Hanson tab 223. This is a document we recently saw in the cross-examination of one of your witnesses. This is a transcript in July or August of 1994, and this is an interview with -- between Mr. Risto Djogo and Jovan Tintor. Now, I want to confirm two things before we explore this document, Mr. Krajisnik. Jovo Tintor had a close relationship with your family. I think the term in your language is "kum." Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was kum to one of my relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which means that there was a close relationship between one of your relatives and Mr. Tintor; correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They were close.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Which relative is that?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Krajisnik Slavka Slavisa. I'm his paternal uncle, twice removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you knew Mr. Tintor, didn't you, before the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And Mr. Tintor was also, as we have seen earlier, a member of the SDS Main Board with you. And in this interview, Mr. Krajisnik, I'm referring to the English page 5, starting at the top; and, Mr. Krajisnik, for your benefit, in the B/C/S it is the page that has the ERN number with the last four digits 5236. You may remember this interview, Mr. Krajisnik. This is where Mr. Djogo reveals a secret and asks Mr. Tintor about essentially a ruse that he employed prior to the beginning of the war where he and his ex-secretary, Ms. Branka, loaded up a procession of 32 vehicles, they loaded them up with weapons, pretended it was a wedding procession, and they smuggled those weapons into the municipality of Vogosca. Now, I want to establish one other fact with you, Mr. Krajisnik. This Branka was your interpreter, wasn't she, in various negotiations?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. No. No. This is his secretary. Nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Did you know Ms. Branka?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No way. I know who that person is. I had nothing to do with her.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: This person who was a witness, as far as this case is concerned, was in Sarajevo before as an interpreter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Krajisnik, first of all, this -- this episode where 32 vehicles containing weapons were smuggled into Vogosca, first of all, how far is Vogosca from your home in Rajlovac?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if he went from Pale, he went a completely different way, as if he went via Washington. Vogosca is perhaps four or five kilometres away, perhaps even less. Well, yes, it is five kilometres away from Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, again, Mr. Krajisnik, as you will see in P1001, according to General Kukanjac's report, 1.500 weapons were distributed to persons in the municipality of Vogosca. Did -- Mr. Krajisnik, did Mr. Tintor ever discuss with you this episode of which he was quite proud and which he publicly revealed his -- his happiness over this event? Did he ever discuss that with you or any other event relating to arming prior to the beginning of the war?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did not discuss it, Mr. Prosecutor. Had he discussed it, he probably would have given weapons to my people from Zabrdje. They wouldn't have got it from Rajlovac on the eve of the war. On the map, I see that it couldn't go through Rajlovac at all. It had to take a different route, via Kobilja Glava, if this was actually the case, what he says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Let's turn to a different document, Mr. Krajisnik. It's found at tab 119. This has an exhibit number already. This is P893, tab 3. Mr. Krajisnik, this has exhibited in this court before. You have a copy of it. This is a document from the 2nd Military District Command. It's 2nd of March, 1992. It's entitled "Hand-over of an automatic rifle of 7.62-millimetre calibre." It's to the command of the 1st Artillery Battalion of the Anti-tank Battalion, and it is signed by General Kukanjac. And it says in the relevant part, it says: "Based on the need and current situation in the city of Sarajevo you have to issue to the Territorial Defence Staff of Novo Sarajevo the following," and it describes 250 automatic rifles of 7.62-millimetre calibre. Again, very quickly, Mr. Krajisnik, Novo Sarajevo, how far -- first of all, that's the contiguous municipality to Novi Grad where Rajlovac is located; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know how far away that is? That's a city municipality, Novo Sarajevo, and then Novi Grad, and then Rajlovac is after that. It would be a good thing if you looked at the map. It's not nearby at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Well --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps 10 kilometres, 12.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. We'll take a look --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Far away from Rajlovac.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: We have the maps, Mr. Krajisnik. We can examine those at a later time. In P1001, Mr. Krajisnik, again the annex to General Kukanjac's report of March 20th, it indicates that 2.800 weapons had been distributed prior to March the 20th, 1992. Now, I'll ask you the same question, Mr. Krajisnik: In this municipality, and it was very close to your municipality, were you aware at all that arms had been distributed by the SDS or the JNA to members of that particular municipality?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you that I don't know about any supplies of arms from the Yugoslav People's Army except from Rajlovac. I only know when they provided arms to Zabrdje and Sokolje from Rajlovac. And you can see here automatic rifle 7.62. That is the Russian Kalashnikov. And that's the difference between that and "automat," an automatic weapon. This is a modern Russian rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Pardon me, Your Honour. I'm going to be referring to the 10th session of the Bosnian Serb Assembly, and if that could be distributed. Your Honours, I'm going to be referring to page 6 in the English, the first full paragraph on page 6 of the English. It is five lines from the bottom of that paragraph, starting with the word "Fortunately ..." Mr. Krajisnik, for your benefit, that will be found on page 7 of the B/C/S. That first full paragraph, about midway through. I'm going to be referring to this portion of the Assembly session. And in this 10th session of the Assembly, which was on the 11th of March, 1992, Mr. Krajisnik, in this case Mr. Karadzic says, and I quote: "Fortunately, we have not relied on those talks but have been putting in place the prerequisites necessary for the security of the Serbian people in its ethnic regions in BH to prevent them from leading us on. They did not succeed in that because we did not omit to take all the steps necessary for the protection of the Serbian people." Now, you were present at that session, Mr. Krajisnik. When Dr. Karadzic refers to putting in place the prerequisites necessary for the security of the Serbian people and not omitting to take all necessary steps for the protection of the Serbian people, what did you understand Dr. Karadzic to be talking about on March the 11th, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Here he was talking about a document that the MPs did not want to accept. And they didn't accept it at this session. I chaired the session only in part. As far as I can remember, it was the vice-president who was chairing it, because they imputed to me that I would be talking the MPs into not accepting the document. So I spent that entire session resigned, as I feel today while giving testimony to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: When you say you didn't chair that session, were you physically present in that session?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I probably was present, yes. I'm not trying to say that I left the hall, but I'm telling you what the point of the session was. So the main point was the Brussels paper, not whether something was provided, whatever. What he was saying here -- well, it's just talk in order to sell this paper, this document. I don't know what he meant. Perhaps he meant arming too. I have no idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: He's clearly not talking about, Mr. Krajisnik, just the talks, because he starts his sentence by saying, "Fortunately, we have not relied on those talks. We've taken other steps." My question to you is what other steps was he talking about, Mr. Krajisnik?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only thing we can do is find Karadzic and bring him here and ask him. I think that's the only solution. There is no other solution.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know what steps he meant. How can I interpret that? "Regionalisation," what did he mean? "Arming," whatever. I don't know what he meant. But this is a debate that is supposed to calm people down. Hundreds of things can be brought under this heading, believe me. Of course, you're thinking about arming because the topic here today is arming.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krajisnik, since these remarks were delivered on the 11th of March, let's take a look at tab 106, and we might get some insight into what Dr. Karadzic was talking about when he said that --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- [Previous translation continues] ... was necessary for the security of the Serbian people had been taken and all steps necessary for their protection had been taken. You will find at tab 106 - this is P51 - this is a document that's been exhibited on many occasions here, Mr. Krajisnik. I specifically refer you to -- the Court, the Chamber, to page 4 of the English, sub-part 5. And, Mr. Krajisnik, that will be found in the B/C/S at page 4, sub-part 5. It's at the bottom of the page. In conjunction with that document, Mr. Krajisnik, I am going to refer you also to tab 107, which is P1001. Mr. Krajisnik --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: -- you know this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know this document. No problem. I know both.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, this document, you'll see the first part of -- the first sentence in page -- sub-part (5), it says: "The map and the key to it show in great detail the volunteer units in the 2nd Military District zone. In this regard, the following must be noted," and it goes on to note that there are volunteer units that are not part of the JNA or TO, comprised of 69.198 persons. It further goes on to say in sub-part (f), it says that "The JNA distributed 51.900 weapons (75 per cent) and the SDS 17.298 weapons." In sub-part (g), in Sarajevo, it says: "To date, 300 automatic weapons have been distributed to retired military officers in Sarajevo..." Now, if we take a look as well, Mr. Krajisnik, at P1001, which is found at tab 107, if you look at items 1 through 9, this is the key that is being referred to by General Kukanjac at the beginning of his -- paragraph 5. And you can see the number of volunteers that are associated with each of those municipalities in Sarajevo, including the municipality of Novi Grad in Sarajevo. And based on General Kukanjac's report to his superiors, you can see, Mr. Krajisnik, that a considerable number of weapons had been distributed in the Sarajevo municipality, including the municipality of Novi Grad. I take it, Mr. Krajisnik, these are facts and events about which you were completely unaware prior to the 12th of May, 1991 -- 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, you're right on that. But I can just tell you one thing: Mr. Kukanjac is dead. But when the investigators asked him about this report, his answer was, "This was written by people. I don't know what this was all about. I just signed it." I cannot understand that he knew about illegal distribution of weapons by the SDS. How could he possibly know about distribution of arms by the SDS if that happened? It is so logical. Allegedly people who dealt with security matters and who worked for him wrote this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Krajisnik, let's take a look at the same page, page 4 of the English. And in the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, I want to refer you to page 4 as well. I'm talking about sub-part (c) on page 4 of the English. It's the second full paragraph. Mr. Krajisnik, it's at the top of the page of page 4 and ends before sub-part (4). And this paragraph, Mr. Krajisnik, describes some problems that the army is having with some representatives of the Bosnian Serbs, but on the whole it says -- and it says: "As a whole, the SDS leadership and the Serbian people accept the army, protect it whenever it is actually possible, join combat and volunteer units, cooperate with the commands as much as possible, treat strategic war materiel in a fairly responsible manner, et cetera." And the last paragraph in that sub-part (c) says: "In this regard, the commander of the 2nd Military District -" that's General Kukanjac, of course - "will soon be talking to the leaders of the Serbian people (Karadzic, Koljevic, Plavsic, Krajisnik, Djukic)."

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Would you just tell me what page this is? I can't find it. I do know that it exists, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: B/C/S page 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I thought I had directed you there, Mr. Krajisnik, but take a look at page 4 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Page 6. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Page 4, not page 6.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got a bit upset with you, but please forgive me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It's page 4, Mr. Krajisnik. If you take a look --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it. I found it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I invite my learned friend to read the sentence he omitted, including the words in brackets.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I tried to cover that by -- at the beginning of the question by saying that there is some criticism of the -- of the army through -- criticism of the SDS by the army. That's what I tried to capture. I don't particularly care to read it. This has been exhibited a number of times, Mr. Krajisnik is familiar with the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I've drawn it to Mr. Krajisnik's attention. It's just arguable, on reading the English, that the answer -- the words "in this regard" relate to the sentence that's been omitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, before you answer any question, you are specifically invited to include in your reading the last three lines of the first paragraph of page 4 which is between brackets, which precedes the announcement of talks to be held with, among others, you. You've seen that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, next question to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, did you have that meeting with General Kukanjac that he foreshadowed in this document?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that there never was such a meeting. I was with Mr. Kukanjac once. I talked to him there, but I don't know who all the attendees were. And I don't know what the time was. March. Well, maybe. Just before the war started, or was it after the war started? I don't know exactly. I did have a meeting with Mr. Kukanjac once. Karadzic was there, I know, but I don't know if the rest were there. I cannot guarantee that. As for the thing up here that the Presiding Judge warned me about, all of this is right. There were different statements in the Assembly, Chetnik ideology and so on and so forth, but that was not the prevalent feature. It is true that the army was criticised, yes. I mean, unfoundedly, but people criticised it. They wanted a Serb army; it's not a Serb army, it's a communist, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, I am looking at the clock.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This is a perfectly good time to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break until 20 minutes past four.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse, I was informed there was something you had on your mind, but I don't know whether this would be the moment to raise it or that you'd rather keep it for a later moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm in Your Honours' hands. It relates briefly to the destruction material, and it's simply this and I appreciate that this may be viewed as somewhat impertinent. It's not intended to be, but it may help -- it would help the Defence if the Chamber are prepared to tell us why the Chamber are anxious to have this material. Of course I'm not expecting an answer now. It's simply because there are various technical objections that we could take. Mr. Krajisnik has objections of slightly more substance, but as much guidance as the Chamber are prepared to give us would really be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And we'll inform you. Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, we ended the session examining P51 and P1001, General Kukanjac's March 20th document, his report to his superiors. I'd like to turn your attention to tabs 122 and 123.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And if I could get an exhibit number on, first of all, tab 122.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P1215, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And an exhibit number for tab 123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, these are documents that are very short, and we will start with P1215 and we'll turn to P1216 because they're related documents. P1215 is a document that is issued from the command of the 10th Corps. It is dated the 23rd of April, 1992. In other words, it's beyond the time of General Kukanjac's report. And it is to the 2nd Military District Command. It is signed by the assistant commander for logistics, it looks like Colonel Grujo Boric, and it says that: "The Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa ask the command of the 530th logistics base and the 10th Corps for help in establishing units and providing them with quartermaster material supplies and equipment and materiel (primarily weapons and ammunition). "Bearing in mind the order of the Federal Secretary for National Defence -" and it gives a number and a date - "and the current political situation in the territory of this municipality, we believe that they should be granted certain material supplies, which would be issued by the 530th POB." If you take a look at tab 123, this is dated the following day. It is from the 2nd Military District Command. It's dated the 24th of April, to the 10th Corps Command and the 530th Logistics Brigade personally to the commander, and it's signed by General Kukanjac. And it relates to the previous document, as you can see, in the -- in the heading, regarding the particular telegram, which it identifies by number. And it says: "Bearing in mind the urgency of implementing the task of establishing the TO units of the Serbian municipality of Bosanska Krupa, and in accordance with the order of the Federal Secretary for National Defence, strictly confidential number 359-1, dated 21 February, 1992, arms, ammunition, and equipment for the newly established TO units in the SO Bosanska Krupa are to be issued from surpluses in units of the 10th Corps and the available stock of the 530th logistics base." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, this, first of all, refers to an order of the Federal Secretariat of National Defence. Do you know what that particular order was?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know what kind of order it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: All right. Were you aware, sir, that General Kukanjac, after the report that he issued found at P51 was continuing to issue supplies to Serbian units, in this case in the municipality of Bosanska Krupa?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know of any of these incidents. If I might just add to what you said. You skipped one word in what you've just read; TO. That means Territorial Defence. I don't know whether it matters or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No, I -- I read it literally what it said, and TO, what it means is identified in the English version. Thank you, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Now, let me turn to the exhibit that's found in tab 124.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: This needs a number as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1217, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, this is a document dated the 24th of April, 1992, from the 2nd Military District Command. It is a document that is signed by General Kukanjac once again. It's directed to the Federal Secretariat of National Defence, the technical administration, and it reads, the first paragraph: "We have received from the Ministry of the Interior of the Serbian Republic of BH a request -" it gives the number - "dated 23 April, 1992, for materiel and technical equipment to be used by the special purposes police detachment of the Banja Luka Security Services Centre. The following equipment has been requested ..." and it identifies in the subsequent pages and in this page equipment that includes a helicopter, an M18 transport helicopter, armoured vehicles of various sorts including combat armoured vehicle. If we go down to weapons, starting at number 9 you'll see a variety of weapons, including machine-guns, automatic rifles of various calibre, pistols, et cetera. If you -- all the way between item number 9 and item number 29 are various forms of weapons or explosives or grenades and the like. And at the end of this document, Mr. Krajisnik, General Kukanjac informed the Federal Secretariat of National Defence - and I'm referring to the paragraph directly above the signature block: "We think that the request should be met primarily with equipment that cannot be found on the market and in quantities that can cover the most essential needs." Mr. Krajisnik, you said you didn't know that the JNA was arming the Bosnian Serbs. In this case, this is a request that the JNA received from the minister of interior of the Serbian Republic of BH for considerable logistical equipment and arms. Were you aware of this request by the minister of the interior?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of it. I was not informed. He was able to do that on his own without letting me know. And war had been going on for already 20 days by this date. And from this I see that the JNA wasn't providing weapons except maybe on an individual basis, because from this we see that they didn't have any weapons. The police, I mean, if they were requesting this amount. And war had been going on for 20 days by this time. Plus I want to say another thing. On the 7th of April an order was issued by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia-Herzegovina to besiege all barracks of the JNA. They proclaimed the JNA to be a hostile army, an occupier, and of course the civilian authorities of Republika Srpska were the only authorities on which JNA could rely for support and equipment. And by the way, an enormous amount of equipment and even factories and plants and entire barracks remained in Visoko, Vitez, and other areas that ended up in Muslim hands when the war began.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour, on this topic. Mr. Krajisnik, thank you. I'm going to yield the floor to Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one, perhaps, Mr. Harmon, before we continue. I don't know whether it should be resolved by asking Mr. Krajisnik, but at the end of this document reference is made to a confidential order dated the 30th of December, 1992, which is a bit surprising if the document itself dates from the 24th of April, 1992. And if you look at the semi-last page. If you'll have any explanation or whether this is a mistake. I have not compared with the other documents where confidential orders are mentioned as well, and I do not have any recollection whether such orders, confidential orders, are already in evidence, yes or no. If you'd please pay some attention to that and inform the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I will. And if I may have just one moment, Your Honour, maybe I can reconcile that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the original it's on the -- in the B/C/S version it's on the top of page 4, where it also says the 30th of December, 1992. I thought perhaps it would be a typo in the translation, but it seems not to be that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may direct Your Honours' attention to tab 123.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It appears to be a typo. That would be my observation. But if you look in 123, in the upper left-hand corner - that's Prosecution Exhibit 1216 - this is from the same author, General Kukanjac, it has a strictly confidential number of 31-103-40-1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The document that's before -- that's 1217 is 31-103-41.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that's from --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: So it appears to be the same day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but nevertheless, the December 1992, at the very end of P1217, I can't --

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I can then direct Your Honours' attention to 1216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: The bottom of the paragraph. 1216.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: You'll see the last line refers to a strictly confidential number of 30 December -- a document 2268-1, dated 30 December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: And at the bottom of 1217, page 3, it also refers to strictly confidential number 2268-1, dated 30 December, 1992. So it appears that the 2 is a typographical error.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the original, you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That, at least at first, it sounds reasonable. If there's any issue there, I'll hear from you, Mr. Stewart, or Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Mr. Krajisnik, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We'll make this transition as efficient as possible, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, just for our information, do you intend to rely also on Mr. Harmon's bundle or could we leave that tomorrow, because --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Is there an index with the bundle that has just been handed out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact it's distributed.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: It varies. Perhaps I could have it on the terms I've agreed with Mr. Harmon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Krajisnik.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
