utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, as you will recall during the course of your examination-in-chief, you were asked and answered several questions concerning paramilitaries, including the last two times that I recall would be on the 22nd of May when there was a question about Arkan at approximately page 23, beginning line 24, and you indicated that from this distance everybody thinks that Arkan was well known. Then you continued a little bit about meeting him briefly in Banja Luka and said that, "As a matter of fact, I can say that he was an anonymous person." And then on the 24th of May, at page 86, line 15, in response to a more general question about paramilitaries, you stated, "I was deeply against any paramilitaries. I have no further comment to make." So I'd like to ask you some questions about paramilitary or volunteer groups. First of all, with respect to volunteer groups or paramilitary groups, either from outside Bosnia-Herzegovina or inside, such as Arkan's men or Seselj's group, had you heard of and were you aware of these groups in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were facing the problem of reports from the army that certain paramilitary units were in existence. Let me just explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. I think we'll move a little quicker if we can, to the extent possible, respond yes or no. If my subsequent questions require --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot answer with yes or no. I can just tell you that we discussed the problem, but I have to tell you also why we discussed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, you don't have to tell me that unless you're asked that, Mr. Krajisnik, and then if you want to add that to the end of your testimony, you can, but please listen to my questions and try to answer it. Okay. Now, I understand from your answer that you were aware of reports from the army concerning certain paramilitary groups. First of all, let me make it even more specific: Were you aware of the existence of Arkan's group or Seselj's group in 1991 and 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in 1991 there was no war, so I'm wondering if there's a mistake in your question. In 1991, 1992, I knew about paramilitary units. We -- we didn't know whose paramilitary units they were. We discussed the problem of paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you've made that clear in responses to two questions. Let me make it even more specific: Arkan's group, did you know of their existence in 1991? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether I knew. I told you I -- in 1995, I met Arkan for the first time and spent five minutes with him. I heard from Mrs. Plavsic that she had been there, that she kissed with him. That's all I know. But that's all I know about Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. So you knew of the existence of Arkan and his group in 1992 but only from that reference by Mrs. Plavsic that you just mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, no. From those two incidents I heard about Arkan, I didn't know what kind of unit he had, what they were doing. It's only here and later, generally speaking, in 1995 and 1997 and once I came here, that I learnt a lot of other things.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not going to do this kind of explaining too often but maybe it's helpful here. You'll probably notice that I didn't ask you precisely what kind of unit he had or what they were doing. We really will find it easier, I think, if you listen to the question and just try to answer the question I've asked. Now, what about Seselj's group? Were you aware of their existence in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard the Serb Radical Party bragging that they were sending in volunteers. I heard that, but I never saw them, and I didn't know whether there were any. But I can tell you what volunteers were. There's a difference between volunteers and paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What do you consider the difference between volunteers and paramilitary units coming from outside the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very simple, and I'll put it very briefly. Serbs in Serbia did not easily respond to mobilisation calls, and a loophole was found in the law; namely, that people could volunteer to be mobilised. So they did not fall under official mobilisation, they were mobilised as volunteers. And certain parties, certain political parties, helped rally these volunteers, and they were supposed to be under the command of the JNA, whereas paramilitary units were self-styled warriors who were not officially organised, who came in to wage war, and it happened maybe that somebody from a particular municipality invited them. But even with respect to those units who had come on their own, of their own accord, even with respect to them, we asked that they be put under JNA command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. And with respect to the terminology you've just used, did you consider Arkan's group or -- or Seselj's group to be volunteers or paramilitaries?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't give them any thought at all. I only heard that certain political parties sent in volunteers. They gathered groups, got them mobilised, and they were coming in under the command of the JNA. But I wasn't thinking about Arkan at all. He was in BH on that one occasion when Mrs. Plavsic met with him, and after that, as far as I know, he wasn't in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I think your answer to earlier questions probably embraced a response to this question, but I just want to be clear. Did you know whether Arkan's group or Seselj's group had been involved in activities in Croatia on behalf of Serbs in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm interrupting for this reason, Your Honour: The last answer Mr. Krajisnik gave, he really only answered the question in relation to Arkan. That's not surprising because it was two questions in one. My learned friend's done the same again. He really needs to separate Arkan's group from Seselj's group so we get a clear answer from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, any problem in separating?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you heard the exchange, so we'll break it down. Did you know whether Arkan's group was involved in the war in Croatia on behalf of Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only knew that the Yugoslav People's Army was involved in the Republic of Serb Krajina, that is, in Croatia. And I know that some volunteers were active also, but I thought they were under the JNA. I didn't know to which group they belonged or where they had come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the same question with respect to Seselj's group. Same answer?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: The same, exactly the same, as far as the Republic of Serb Krajina and Croatia is concerned. I know of some -- Captain Dragan, but I don't know what kind of unit he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to your comment in your examination-in-chief about Arkan's anonymity, I just wanted to take a quick look at tabs 146 and 147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Numbers to be assigned to them, I take it, Mr. Tieger?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, tab 146 should be -- would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1218, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is there a translation of this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One second, please. And 147, Madam Registrar, would be?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, about translations. I see in the book -- Mr. Tieger, I -- 146, I do not see any B/C/S translation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there's no translation for 148 either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, we have not come to 148, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't know whether Mr. Krajisnik meant 147.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I don't know either.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Although 148 seems to have a translation problem as well possibly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But we have two problems now. Let's wait for the third one.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, first of all, one can be completely confident that if there are tabs that do not contain translations, they will almost certainly be the first ones to which you turn in the binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It's good to --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Secondly -- and secondly, I think it's possible to proceed at this moment with those documents. If it becomes impossible, we'll try another approach, but if the Court will permit me to make that effort, we'll see how we proceed. And of course we'll obtain a subsequent --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of course. First of all, we have allowed now and then the Defence to do a similar thing, and of course it very much depends on how important the context is. I take it that both Mr. Stewart and Mr. Josse are alert on any --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: The only problem is of course we haven't had a chance to read this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I suppose if Your Honour would give me two minutes to scan it, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's not a problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So we can scan it as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Tieger is punishing me now for not having learned English. He's right on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You can punish him now and then for not having learned B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Having generally familiarised yourselves - and I'm referring, of course, to my learned friends and the Chamber - would it be helpful if I addressed everyone's attention to the particular passages in question resulting?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it it's the bottom of the second page where you mainly are focusing on, and the top of the third page.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It's actually one portion on the first page, the bottom of that, and -- correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'll listen to the question, if I may, and reserve my position, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, I appreciate that. I just didn't think that represented a change in position generally, but I understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At least now, Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I appreciate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- knows now what to object against --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- if it's after the question, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, and I appreciate the fact that there is no translation in front of you, so I'll try to be as clear and brief as possible. Tab 146 contains an article by The Los Angeles Times on December 16, 1991. It refers to -- in the fourth paragraph of that article, to Serbian guerrillas in occupied Croatia doling out favours and boasting of actions in which they liquidated returning Croats. And on the second page, after a longer discussion --

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: One observation: Please could my learned friend go slowly so this is accurately and fully translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's a good point. Will do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: On the second page, at the fifth paragraph from the bottom, the article states: "That view is underscored by Arkan, a renowned guerrilla leader and reputed Belgrade underworld figure whose elite Serbian Tigers claim to fight Fascism and take no prisoners." And then the second article is dated January 4, 1992. That's at tab 147. It's from the Associated Press, and in its third paragraph it states: "As Croatian and federal commanders signed the latest truce Thursday evening, one of Serbia's many camouflage-clad heroes, known by his nom de guerre Arkan, was on prime time Serbian TV news. 'We should not delude ourselves,' said the man called 'the Roman centurian' by an adoring Serbian press. 'The cease-fire results only in the enemy arming and preparing themselves better.'" Then two paragraphs down, the article continues: "The war in secessionist Croatia has brought fame to men like Arkan whose real name is Zarko Raznjatovic." We know that's not the correct first name. "He is a Belgrade cafe owner who heads the Serbian Volunteer Guard, a force of murky origin and size." Now, Mr. Krajisnik, isn't it -- don't these articles - and I don't think there's much dispute that they aren't the only two articles written about Arkan during that time - reflect his notoriety not only in the region but indeed worldwide and that virtually everyone in the region knew about Arkan at that time?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As far as I'm concerned, Mr. Tieger, with all due respect, I am not among the number of people who knew Arkan the way you describe him. I didn't know any of this. I've read it, but I was not informed, and I could not watch TV Belgrade in January in Sarajevo, if that is Serb television.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, if I could ask you to turn to 154, tab 154. That's a very short article from Oslobodjenje on 25 March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: It also needs a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1220, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: P1220 is an article from Oslobodjenje on 25 March, 1992, the title of the article is "Seselj's and Arkan's Men Arrive," and it begins: "Rumours that groups of the so-called Seselj's and Arkan's men were arriving in the Banja Luka region have been confirmed today. Members of those units were seen in Banja Luka and we have unofficially learned that they were deployed along the Krajina border lines," and it goes on to talk about a confirmation, perhaps ambiguous confirmation, by Mr. Cavic.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm far from certain that Mr. Krajisnik could find the place, and in addition to that, if one looks at the B/C/S, it's almost illegible.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't find it. Can you just tell me where this is in the original? I'll look it up straight away.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I believe if you look to the left column -- it's a small article. Far left column, second article.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. "Seselj's Men Arrived," yes. Yes, I've seen it. Afterwards. Oh, yes, yes. Thank you very much to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's so short, perhaps you'd read all of it, Mr. Tieger, unless --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. I'll continue from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The beginning we have had, so then we continue with "ambiguously ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: "Ambiguously, this has been confirmed today by Nikodin Cavic, president of Seselj's SRS of BiH with its seat in Banja Luka. Its leadership has moved today to its new premises in the building of the Municipal Assembly, the entrance from Marsal Tito Street. He did not specify, however, the size of those 'forces' or where they had been deployed but neither did he deny their presence and their dispatching in the direction of Bosanski Brod, Travnik, Jajce, and elsewhere in the Banja Luka region. Who had invited Arkan's and Seselj's men to come over here and why are they now in this part of the Bosnian Krajina?"

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, among other things we can see in that article that there's no explanation of who Seselj's -- who Seselj is, who Arkan is, or what those groups are about, which would appear to suggest that it was written and disseminated -- and it was written by someone confident that the readers would know full well who those groups are. And I ask again if it wasn't the case that by early 1992 Arkan and Seselj and their forces were well known across Bosnia and Herzegovina and indeed the Balkan region?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is not correct, but just look at the next article, the three municipalities in Vlasenica. Until I came here, I didn't know that there were three municipalities in Vlasenica. Just down here. It says that there were three municipalities formed in Vlasenica. I didn't know about that either. I never read this article.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm sure there are many things to which we could point in any particular newspaper article, Mr. Krajisnik, about which there would be no expectation you would be aware. So I'd appreciate it if you wouldn't deflect from the question I've asked. This article talks about Arkan in a way that seems to suggest that all of the readers will know exactly who those groups are, and that's why I'm asking you, isn't true that everybody knew who Arkan and Seselj were and who -- and what their forces were about?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether others knew. I knew of Mr. Seselj. As for Arkan, I told you what I knew. And you gave me an example here which shows that I could have known of Arkan, but I'm telling you underneath that there is this piece of news that I also could have been aware of about the three municipalities in Vlasenica, but I hadn't read that either and I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, let's not -- let's not try to explain everything by logic. This is not an invitation to ignore logics, but we have not seen that article. What Mr. Tieger puts to you is that the news is that they arrived without any further explanation as to who they are. Might well be that in the next article there was some other news that you were not aware of. The issue is - and that's the question Mr. Tieger puts to you - it -- as he says, it appears that upon the news of their arrival in Banja Luka, there was no need for the readers to receive further explanation as to who they were, and you're invited to -- whether or not you would agree that the text presumes knowledge of the average reader of what these groups are. Please proceed -- please comment, and if you have any further comment apart from the comment you gave already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If an average reader read this, he can infer that these were - how should I put this? - units that were against the Muslims, probably since they were in the Krajina. Now, this is Oslobodjenje, so this is a message to the Muslims. But I'm telling you, I never read this article. So if this is an example of me knowing a bit more about Arkan, I would have read the article underneath too.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I do ask again that these two individuals are split up for the purpose of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Krajisnik answered already that he knew Mr. Seselj and that he was not acquainted with Mr. Arkan. And I also -- I think that as far as their groups are concerned that he had no specific knowledge of those groups. He -- I think in his answer he very much focused on the persons rather than the groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Absolutely, Your Honour. That's why I didn't interrupt at the time. I'm just asking that that be done from now on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you're invited to always make a clear distinction between Seselj -- Mr. Seselj and Mr. Arkan and between their groups. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the purpose of clarification, Mr. Krajisnik, you heard the Judge's synopsis of those earlier answers, consistent with my recollection as well, but is that accurate; that is, that you knew Mr. Seselj, you were not acquainted with Mr. Arkan, and you have no specific knowledge of those groups?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware of the whole problem with Seselj, how they threw him out and that the Muslims were afraid of him and how he was revered and -- I'm talking about Seselj. Oh, you're asking me about Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No. You heard what I asked you. I asked you that very -- I recited what the Court had summarised as your previous answer and just asked you if that was right. I didn't ask you for everything you knew about Seselj at the time.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Did I know of Seselj? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's try to get things clear. I think you're -- you testified, Mr. Krajisnik, that you knew Mr. Seselj, and you added to that that you knew about the -- the whole problem with Mr. Seselj and how they threw him out. Did you know about any group, whether volunteers or paramilitaries, that operated under, well, let's say Mr. Seselj's flag or Mr. Seselj's name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, yes. I've already said that he reduced this. They had some kind of insignia and whatever, but they were under the army of Republika Srpska in Sarajevo during the war, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think as a matter of fact we're now talking about the 25th of March, 1992. At least, Mr. Tieger, that's how I understood it, your question to relate to the moment of --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about that. I don't know about that date, but in the war, yes. At the Jewish cemetery in Sarajevo there was a unit that called themselves the Chetnik unit, but they were under the army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And that was after March, I take it. After March, 1992.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Line 9. It is not "reduced" but "recruited."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So in your terminology there were volunteers rather than paramilitaries. The same question now for any group under the -- under the flag or under the name of Mr. Arkan. That is, were you aware, late March of 1992, of such a group to exist?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not aware of any of that except for Bijeljina. Well, I didn't know about Bijeljina, but I knew later on the basis of reports. I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, when you referred to troops at the Jewish cemetery under the Chetnik unit, as you called them. Did you consider them to be Arkan's men or Seselj's men, or did you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Seselj's, Seselj's. They were members of his party. But they were under the army, under the command of the army, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And taking -- moving from the Court's question about late March, 1992, at any point in 1992 were you aware of groups operating under the flag or name of Arkan operating in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not know about that, although I heard some conversations here. I didn't know about this. This was completely unknown to me that that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: What paramilitary or volunteer groups did you know about that were operating in Bosnia and Herzegovina - and that is Serbian paramilitary or volunteer groups - in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know anything specific, but I told you the army was saying at some meeting, "We have units that are not under anybody's command but under the municipal authorities," and orders were being issued. I didn't know of a unit. I mean, if somebody were to mention it to me, perhaps I would say, yes, I heard of that unit. I mentioned that thing in Herzegovina, Karadjordje, if you remember. I heard of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Let's turn to tab 136.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a document we've seen before. It's P529, tab 463. It's a strictly confidential report dated July 28, 1992, by then Colonel Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And Mr. Krajisnik, at the very first paragraph of that document, Colonel Tolimir lists or specifies a number of such groups, including the Arkanovci, Arkan's men; Seseljovci, Seselj's men; Captain Dragan's commandos; Captain Oliver's commandos; Carli's men; Jovic's men; White Eagles; the Wolves, and so on. Now, looking at those specified groups, were you aware of the existence of those groups and their operation in -- on the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will tell you who I never heard of. Never heard of Oliver's commandos, Carli's men, Suva Rebra, "Smoked Ribs," never heard of that. Heard of White Eagles, Arkanovci, Seseljovci. This Captain Dragan, I heard of him but in Republika Srpska Krajina. But not as units, not as units taking part. And I never received this information. See, I even looked at the list of persons this was copied to: The president of the Presidency, the Prime Minister, and the Main Staff, but never mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Okay. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we take it one by one, because Mr. Tieger is invited to -- so you said never heard of Oliver's commandos, Carli's men, the Smoked Ribs, and then heard of White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the others which you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Wolves. I heard of the Wolves. I mean generally speaking in the war. Beli Orlovi, the White Eagles, and Jovicevci is one and the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And did you hear of any of the others? Because the question is now --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've said during the war -- during the war, generally speaking, as a concept, I mean if there was Arkan, there was Arkanovci, but I did not hear that they were there. Seseljovci, I heard of that. Commandos of Captain Dragan; I heard of Captain Dragan, that he was in the Serb Krajina. Vukovi, the Wolves, probably the Wolves from Prnjavor. That's probably what is meant here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you said during the war, the question was limited to 1992. Do you say I heard of those in 1992, or would it -- would it also have been later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, really, with all goodwill, I don't know when I heard of the White Eagles, but like Seselj's men, they were recruited because he had his party, and then volunteers were sent to be under the JNA. Even in 1991. But under the JNA. I don't think that they were in our army, but here I see that they say that they were, so I don't know. There was this problem of paramilitary formations. That we discussed. That I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In the sixth paragraph down on that first page, Mr. Krajisnik, Colonel Tolimir writes that: "One can conclude without reservations that they -" well, that these groups - "are the genocidal element among the Serbian people." Do you have any reason to disagree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, tell me where this is. Is this on page 1? I haven't found it. And if it's not too much trouble, can you tell me where it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Page 1 of the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, yes. Yes. I beg your pardon. Yes, I found it. I think that this part of the sentence is certainly correct, that many paramilitary formations had a strong hatred towards non-Serbs, and they were inclined towards crime. Now, whether this has to do with genocide or not, I cannot say, and that is why we strove for having them under the command of the military or, rather, those who were striving were those under whose jurisdiction this was. But I was present at such a meeting when the Main Staff complained about these problems in municipalities. And also that the morale is poor -- or, rather, that there were some people with poor moral qualities, whereas on the other hand there were some honourable people too.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And you were also present at the meeting of the Presidency on June 9th when the decision was issued banning the establishment and activities of such groups which are not under the central command of the army and the police; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did attend one such meeting when the military made a report that they had a problem with paramilitary units, and it was said in very strict terms that everybody had to be placed under army command and all other units have to be banned. I don't know whether that was that meeting that you are referring to, but I remember that meeting, and I remember being happy with the conclusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Indeed, if you'll turn to tabs 126 and 127 -- I see there's no B/C/S, but this was an original English disseminated by the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: They will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Tab 126 will be Exhibit P1221. Tab 127 will be Exhibit P1222.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, I just made reference to the decision of the Presidency on June 9, 1992, and, if necessary or useful to you, I'll be happy to show you that particular decision, which I know we've seen before in the course of this case. Tab 126 is --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am inclined to believe everything the Prosecutor says, and please write it down as my cooperation with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Tab 126 contains a decision in English stating that the president -- Presidency of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at its session - and it recites the decision in English with three paragraphs, some further elaboration. And then tab 127 contains a letter to the Secretary-General, Dr. Boutros-Ghali on June 13, 1992, informing him about what Dr. Karadzic calls, "Our latest official decision to disown all paramilitary groups that are not ready to be under our political control." And for your benefit, that letter continues: "As you can see, we are trying to stop the tragedy of ethnic conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina at different relevant levels." It states, "The enclosed decision is in accordance with our energetic efforts to stop the war as soon as possible," and then expresses appreciation for the UN's peacekeeping role. I wanted to provide that backdrop, Mr. Krajisnik, because I wanted to ask you why the Bosnian Serb leadership would incorporate within its military forces groups of people with at least violent criminal motivations and tendencies towards non-Serbs, if not genocidal tendencies.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll give you a very simple answer as to what we believed: Every free man in the war, unless under somebody's command, is free to commit illegal acts. If he is placed under somebody's command, that same person can act in a disciplined manner and execute orders. The problem lies not in the man but whether somebody has command over him or he is acting on his own impulses. If you ask me, such people should have been placed in army units. And let me tell you, the -- what Tolimir wrote, those people should have been either expelled or placed under army command. That's what the army should have done. Plavsic, Karadzic or Koljevic were not the ones who were supposed to do that. Why didn't he place those paramilitary units under his command? There was no other armed force that was capable of doing that. I don't understand the letter that he is addressing to somebody else when it's their own jurisdiction. Why didn't he expel them? As for the 13th of June, if you remember, on that date Mr. Subotic wrote instructions that everybody had to act in accordance with Geneva Conventions. That was given to every individual soldier. And it was not a Presidency session that was held. Instead, Mr. Subotic and Mr. Karadzic wrote that instruction individually, and it was published in the Official Gazette. It was given to every single soldier, and that's why Karadzic wrote that letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be obviously moving on, but we're getting close to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, so am I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- running out of the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will have a break until five minutes past six.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, may we go into private session briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, Mr. Krajisnik, Arkan's forces did come to -- not only operated in Zvornik and Bijeljina but came to Sarajevo for the same purpose.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know, although here I saw in an intercept that that is so. That was an intercept between Mladic and Unkovic. I learned about it here, but back then and there, I didn't know. It's probably the municipality that engaged them on their own initiative. What do I know? Let me just remind you, Mladic said on that occasion that everybody has to be placed under the army, and he meant those men who had been brought on somebody's own initiative. But at that time, I didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: In fact, you're referring, Mr. Krajisnik, to an intercepted telephone conversation between Mr. Unkovic and General Mladic on the 13th of May, 1992. That can be --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's a conversation that you played here, and I learned then that there's something in it. But then on the 13th of May, I can't remember I was. Maybe I was travelling. I don't know. Maybe I was in Herzegovina, maybe even in Grac. I have no idea. Yes, I was in Banja Luka. On the 12th of May I was in Banja Luka, and this conversation took place on the 13th.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, the conversation on the 13th of May reflecting Arkan's presence, Mr. Krajisnik, does not mean that's the only date on which Arkan was there or the only date on which you had an opportunity to learn about the presence of his forces there.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm looking at this conversation, and on my list it doesn't appear to have an exhibit number, although I would have thought it would have, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Under what -- is it included in --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It's in one of the additional materials that's ready to be distributed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And -- Mr. Usher, could you please assist. Before we assign a new number, perhaps we could check on whether ... Mr. Tieger, we are just trying to find out whether we have -- meanwhile, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, you received a copy. You seem to be looking at that now. And as it indicates on the second page shortly before the conclusion of the conversation, Professor Unkovic and General Mladic discuss the presence of Arkan's men. And as you indicated, General Mladic indicates that they are under his command, as he says, if they want to stay alive. And Professor Unkovic says, "Excellent. Excellent." Now, in addition to Professor Unkovic from a Crisis Staff member from Ilidza, and General Mladic, there were others who knew as well. For example, Mr. Prstojevic knew that Arkan's forces were present in Sarajevo and operating with the Bosnian Serb forces. And if you look at tab 139 --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And before we go further, Your Honour, that caution was warranted. The previous intercept of May 13, 1992, between Unkovic and Mladic is P529, tab 265.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the intercept at tab 139, the telephone conversation between Mr. Prstojevic and Milisav Gagovic on 14 May, 1992, is P793.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Krajisnik, the relevant portion of that conversation, after some discussion about the operations of the Bosnian Serb forces, the manpower and hardware available, appears at approximately the last quarter of the conversation, about the tenth line from the bottom, where Mr. Prstojevic says: "I do not know for sure if anything is in working order here. Two tanks, three APCs and so on. I'm not sure for this checkpoint. "Gagovic: Fuck! "Prstojevic: And those two yesterday are with Arkan's men." So that's a reflection of the fact again, Mr. Krajisnik, that Arkan's men are operating in Sarajevo and not secretly. So in addition to the highest level of the military command of the -- at least the -- insofar as General Mladic is concerned, down to Mr. Prstojevic, a Crisis Staff commander, and Gagovic as well. So notwithstanding what seems to be, from these intercepts, reasonably well known among those aware of the personnel and activities of the Bosnian Serb forces of the presence of Arkan's forces, it's -- you didn't hear anything about the presence of Arkan -- Arkan's men in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I've told you quite simply that I did not memorise that in any way. I told you about Seselj's men. I knew about them. I didn't know about -- I didn't know about Arkan's men, and I don't even know when this was going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we talked a few moments ago about Zvornik and the awareness of the Bosnian Serb leadership, at least insofar as you were aware, of the events in Zvornik and Arkan's involvement in that. Perhaps we can take a look at how Arkan's forces came to Sarajevo. If we could look at --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Wait a minute. Are you saying that I said that I knew about Arkan's men, or is it something that you are putting to me about Arkan's men being in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It may be a translation problem or perhaps just the way I asked the question, Mr. Krajisnik, but I just referred back to the question and answers we had before about that subject.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I'd like to turn to another additional item, number 4, P292, KID 31230, an intercepted telephone conversation between Mrs. Plavsic and Rus of 23 April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which tab? Could you tell -- ah, yes. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, in this conversation, Mr. Krajisnik, we can see at the top that Mrs. Plavsic calls, announces herself, and asks, "Is Zeljko there?" And is told, "He's not up yet. Mr. Rus is here." Down the page about five lines or so, Rus greets her, "... with deepest respect, madam ... this is Rus," and explains that he is the commander's batman. They continue with Mrs. Plavsic wanting to ask Rus something because, as she puts it, "Zeljko is not there, right?" And then she goes on, "All right. All right. Never mind then. This is what it's about. I've returned here to my base, the one where I'm from." Another passage down: "I haven't arrived home yet. One small part was blocked. But I wanted ... ask him if we ask him to come here if that was possible in theory." Rus, on the next page, indicates that he doesn't have authorisation to speak on behalf of Arkan but will pass him the message immediately. As you can see in the next small passage, they devise a code for that purpose, with Mrs. Plavsic indicating, "I'll just ask if you can possibly bring the merchandise." And Rus says he understands: "Yes, bravo, very clever." And they try to arrange a time when he can call. And then about six lines down, Mrs. Plavsic says: "All right. Tell me, how are things in Zvornik? Can you tell me that?" Rus: "Sorry?"

utterances.speaker: MRS. PLAVSIC
utterances.text: "How are things in Zvornik? Did Pejo go there?" Rus says: "Well, I don't know ... he was supposed to go there as well to visit." She says: "Yes, yes. I know." And he continues: "... the entire situation ... because there are all sorts of rumours." Mr. Krajisnik, this is a reflection of the fact that after witnessing what Arkan did in Bijeljina and learning of what he did in Zvornik, the conclusion was reached that he was the right guy for the job in Sarajevo, and she invited him to come to Sarajevo in that phone call, or prepared to invite him to come to Sarajevo and passed on that invitation. There's no dispute about that, is there?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read this. It was not my understanding that he was supposed to come to Sarajevo, but I know why he was supposed to come to Sarajevo; to get her out of Sarajevo because she herself was under a blockade by the Muslims. That was the reason why he was supposed to come to Sarajevo, Zeljko. And somebody testified about that here. That's how I know. I would like to remind you of the fact that this is the 23rd of April, and if you remember one protected witness, he mentioned that he -- that she was in Lukavica on the 20th of April, that she met him when I claimed that that was not the case, that she was in Sarajevo in her own apartment in Muslim-held territory. And before that, she was in Zvornik with Linda Karadjordjevic, before that, in Zvornik, according to what she wrote in her book. I did not know about that. I had no contact with her at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we can see from the previous intercepts, Mr. Krajisnik, that Arkan's group engaged in activities with the other Bosnian Serb forces regarding things other than some sort of rescue mission for Mrs. Plavsic. Is it your testimony that they stuck around to assist?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, but she made a statement to you that she called Arkan to get her out of Sarajevo. It's in the statement you showed me. In your statement, Mrs. Plavsic was interpreting this conversation, that she was under a blockade by these Muslim gangs.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, my apologies if I led you to talk about the particular document. Of course I'm interested in knowing what you knew at the time. So is it your testimony that despite the --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Despite what General Mladic said at the time, and Mr. Unkovic, and Mr. Prstojevic, and Gagovic, and the others, and now Mrs. Plavsic, that you were never apprised of Arkan's presence in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not apprised of it. I tell you. You can see the transcript of the Assembly of Republika Srpska where Djokanovic and Jovan Mijatovic quarreled about the activities of the Yellow Wasps and Arkan, and he said that that wasn't correct. That is the only knowledge I have about Arkan as far as Zvornik is concerned. Maybe I knew that there were some units, but I didn't relate it to Arkan. How can I know? It was a long time ago. I cannot state anything emphatically. I just told you what I knew about the man Arkan.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, you did refer to Arkan's involvement in -- or the involvement of Arkan's forces in getting Mrs. Plavsic out of Sarajevo, and since you did refer to that, that's found at tab 138. It's a conversation in May between Legija and first -- or between Legion, Erdut --

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. I'm sorry. Excuse me. I didn't say that they were there. I said that Mrs. Plavsic in her statement said that she called Rus so that Arkan would help her get out. Now, I don't know whether that happened, whether he helped her.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, I'm directing your attention to tab 138, which I believe will need a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I was not attentive. The number, Madam Registrar, would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will be P1223, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a conversation, Mr. Krajisnik, as you can see, which begins between two persons named Erdut and Legion, and Legion asks to speak to the commander at the beginning of the conversation and asks to have him passed on, and then --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: There's a bit of an ambiguity here, Your Honour. The heading -- the heading indicates it is a conversation between the three, but as you can see, the listings of the participants just have the first two, notwithstanding the fact that the portion is, "Do pass him on," and then it appears someone comes on the line and says, "How's it going, Legy" We will check who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, who are the interlocutors.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: But in any event, Mr. Krajisnik, as you can see in the middle of that first page they discuss "that female friend of ours Biljana" and the fact that she was liberated. And then if you continue toward the back, they indicate in about 10 lines from the bottom that "there," meaning concluded, "I hope she'll contact Mladic and Karadzic today, there." "So there, we've got it all under control." Did Dr. Karadzic ever make reference to you to his awareness of Arkan's forces operating in Sarajevo or to being contacted shortly after Mrs. Plavsic's release from or departure from Sarajevo in connection with that event?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assert with full certainty that I was not abreast of any of this. And Karadzic -- well, no. I don't remember any of this, no. And also, Arkan wasn't the one who set Biljana Plavsic free. It was the MUP of Republika Srpska. Well, that's what she was boasting of, and how can I know who it was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Now, we've seen a number of intercepts where the persons operating or commanding forces or working with the Bosnian Serb forces from Pale, for example, have numerous exchanges and seem to know each other reasonably well, seem to know who each -- who each other is and what their general role in the Bosnian Serb forces are. Is that a reflection of generally the comparatively small size of Pale? Among other things, of course.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand. Please don't hold it against me, but I do not follow what you're saying or I cannot follow what you're saying. I don't understand the gist of your question. Pale was the centre of the republic, so no dispute about that, although it's a small place. Karadzic was there, the Assembly was there. No dispute about that. If that is an answer to your question. It wasn't some other place.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I wanted to let that question and answer go. In the answer immediately before the last question, the translation says that she was boasting of, presumably, it. I understand that in fact what Mr. Krajisnik said is that the MUP of the Republika Srpska was boasting about it. Perhaps that could be clarified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, who was boasting about having freed, liberated Mrs. Plavsic? Was it Arkan's men or was it -- no, was it Biljana Plavsic, or was it the MUP? Who did say so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The MUP of Republika Srpska. When I talked to them, they said, "We could have all lost our lives on account of Biljana Plavsic."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That being corrected, you may proceed, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I asked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're stuck more or less on your last question, which was, Mr. Krajisnik, where people seem to know each other well in their telephone conversations, does that reflect, especially people in command, does that reflect that Pale was just a small village where everyone knew each other? Is that just --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: At least in part, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] None of these people are from Pale. All of these people here are from Sarajevo, outside Pale. That's why I didn't understand. Gagovic, Mladic, everybody, Prstojevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It maybe helpful to actually wait for the subsequent questions, Mr. Krajisnik. And you did indicate Pale is a small place. I noted earlier in your testimony you spoke about calling up people you knew, according to you, to find out what was going on at the time. Is it fair to say that at least in Pale people, especially those in -- who travelled in circles of higher political or military positions knew each other?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, again, perhaps it's not clear enough to me, but if they were in Pale, then more or less they all met each other even if they hadn't met before. So more or less everybody got to know each other. Ministers and others, if that's what you mean, or are you referring to the municipal organs?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I just wanted to -- to determine whether my general understanding of the size of the place and the number of interactions that would result from that relatively small size was roughly accurate. And I asked that, Mr. Krajisnik, because -- if I could ask you to turn to tab 130.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: It will need a number, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be P1224, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: We see on page 3 of the English at the top -- let me identify what that is first. That's a report from the RS MUP on the realisation of a strictly confidential order that's numbered there, dated August 3, 1992. And as we can see at the second paragraph in the English on page 3 and also at the top of the page in B/C/S on page 3, that about 20 of Arkan's men were staying not only in the general area but at the Panorama Hotel. That's where you lived, Mr. Krajisnik; right?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly weren't staying with me. This is a pure lie. I lived in Panorama. I don't know where they were, but they were not where I was. I don't know who they were. Maybe there were some guests who I didn't know. But that somebody said to me that there were 20 of Arkan's men, that is not correct. Perhaps they were like refugees, because there were lots of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And if we look quickly at tab 131.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And that would need a number as well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: P1225, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: This is a report to the minister of the interior dated August 10, 1992. And again page 3 of the English and page 3 of the B/C/S, Mr. Krajisnik. It confirms that that group of Arkan's men are still at the Panorama Hotel.

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assure you, from day one until my arrest I was in Panorama. Arkan's were never in Panorama. There were refugees like I was. Whether some of the refugees were declared as such, that I don't know, but they were never in Panorama. If there's a different Panorama, then I don't know about it. No way. No way. This is pure fabrication. I don't know if they were staying at some other facility.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: You say it's a fabrication. Is there -- are you aware of some reason why that particular representation would have been fabricated?

utterances.speaker: MOMCILO KRAJISNIK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying -- I'm saying that I know with certainty that refugees were there. I was there too. Next to Panorama there was a small weekend cottage where Karadzic was. I never heard that there were any of Arkan's men there in Panorama throughout that time. There are books from Panorama, so somebody can check this out. I don't know where they could have been. This comes as a sort of shock to me. This is not correct. Maybe among the refugees. Maybe somebody smuggled them in. I don't know. There were a lot of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I submit that that last question was grossly unfair. Two documents have been thrown at the witness, couple of lines, long documents not previously exhibited in the case, and the witness is then asked the question, Well, has all this been fabricated? Excuse me for paraphrasing what my learned friend has said. The witness needs to read the document, perhaps overnight, and then be invited to comment on these documents properly. This is not the proper way to cross-examine, in my submission.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Your Honour, notwithstanding what seems to be undue umbrage by my learned friend, I did not ask -- pose to Mr. Krajisnik the question whether it was fabrication. He raised it, and so I simply asked if he had a basis for that, which seems to me a perfectly fair question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Josse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, the question has been put to you why, what would be the reason for such, as you call it, a fabrication. Mr. Josse very much thought it fair that you could read the whole of the document so that you know at least the context on which this, what you said to be a fabrication, was presented. Mr. Tieger, the Chamber would not mind if Mr. Krajisnik would answer your question tomorrow after he has had an opportunity to read the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Of course, Your Honour. That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. So --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can answer now if you want. I can answer now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you want to answer it now. You always can add something tomorrow, but the question is what would be the reason for someone to put such a fabrication in this report? Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no idea. I can only say that I thought who was sleeping in what room. At first my family, my relatives were there. I never heard that Arkan's men were there in 1992. There. That's what I can say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You repeat that it's not true what is said in this report, but you've answered the question that you have got no idea. You've got no idea why. Yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, there were many refugees. Maybe among them there were such people. I could not identify them then as Arkan's men because everything was overbooked. If that was the case, well, possibly, because then I was struggling with my wife's illness. But I was never aware of Arkan's men in Panorama.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where you earlier said that it's a fabrication, you now say that if it is true, that you did not -- you were not aware of anyone in the hotel, of which you tell us that there were many refugees, that any of them were Arkan's men, although you do not exclude for the possibility that there were. Is that a correct understanding of your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, you asked me about what the reason was for someone to lie. I said I don't know. But if I were to guess, if I were to guess and to help this person who wrote this, then I'm trying to find something, like I didn't know about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But if you didn't know about it, it doesn't mean that someone else does lie. I mean, we have two issues: First whether it's a fabrication, yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You used the word it was a fabrication. That means -- at least, I understand a fabrication to be that someone intentionally said this although it was not true. Then you later on -- at least, I understood your testimony to be a bit different; that is, that although you do not exclude for the possibility, you only identified other guests as many of them being refugees but not excluding for the possibility -- for the possibility that among those refugees there were people who might have been Arkan's men. The reason for the fabrication becomes irrelevant as soon as you do not stick to what was your earlier testimony is that it was a pure fabrication. Please proceed, Mr. Tieger. We've got three minutes left. If you want to start with a new subject --

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I think that would be preferable, Your Honour, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will adjourn for the day, which means, Mr. Krajisnik, that I again -- I again remind -- instruct you not to speak with anyone about the testimony. I know for sure that you know my words by heart already. Just not to speak with anyone about your testimony already given or still to be given, and -- it seems that you wanted to say something before I adjourned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, please? May I ask my investigators tonight to go to Panorama and to see whether Arkan's men were there ever? I was not aware of Arkan's men in 1992, 1993, 1994. Never heard of it. When I'm saying this to you -- when I'm saying that this was a pure fabrication, pure invention, well, it is a strong word. I mean, I should have known that they were there if they were there, but that's why I use such strong wording. May I ask my investigators to go there and to check this out? If there's anyone up there, I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, I'd like to -- it would be at least very unusual that a witness consults with investigators in order to find out whether his own answers, which are just about your knowledge, Mr. Krajisnik -- you did not say that they were not there. I take it -- but, Mr. Tieger, the request of Mr. Krajisnik, would you oppose contact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's it. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, perhaps I could point out we have heard what Mr. Krajisnik has said. We are free to contact the investigators any time we like. Therefore, we can judge -- I think Mr. Tieger has this in mind as well. We can judge and read and decide what to do about it. There is no need for Mr. Krajisnik to contact investigators because we can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, no, no. I was just asking. Mr. Krajisnik asked whether he could do it, and then I invited Mr. Tieger to tell us whether he would oppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm short-circuiting by saying it's completely unnecessary so Mr. Tieger doesn't need to be asked. Mr. Krajisnik doesn't need to do it because we can do it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The next question would be whether you could communicate what you learned from an investigator. But you could use it in re-examination, if you want to.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, that's sort of what I had in mind, Your Honour, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's clear. I expected, as a matter of fact, that you would oppose, Mr. Tieger, that Mr. Krajisnik -- but now we are --

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: He doesn't need to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I was going to say yes, I would oppose, and particularly because there is such an appropriate expedient available otherwise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I am glad we were able to clear that up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No, it's not the same thing when Mr. Stewart asks and when I ask. My conversations are recorded, and I will say look at this, look at this, and look at this, so you will have all of it. It's not that I'm saying there go there and take this, take that period, take that period, whatever. Because Mr. Stewart is just going to say were Arkan's men there? That's not sufficient. Record the conversation that I'm going to have. But then if it's not necessary, then it's not necessary. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krajisnik, your request is denied, and as you may have heard, of course Defence counsel is in a position --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- to put the questions in whatever way they would like to your investigators to the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's all right. I agree. I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just say so there is no misunderstanding as Mr. Krajisnik goes off for the evening, naturally, as always my intervention was intended to help Mr. Krajisnik. I hope he understands that. I think he does now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, you're right. You're right. I was revolted, and I wanted to double-check on myself, because I don't know whether they were there. But I agree with you. If somebody believes it, then they believe it. I agree with you. It's all right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll then adjourn for the day. Where we thought that we would adjourn at three minutes to 7.00, it's now three minutes past 7.00. We'll adjourn until tomorrow, quarter past two, same courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 8th day of June, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24
